reference: Yang et al. (2021), Testing (Quizzing) Boosts Classroom Learning, DOI 10.1037/bul0000309
scope: classroom testing; 222 studies; 48,478 students
key_finding: Quizzing improved classroom achievement on average; effects varied with feedback, repetition, format consistency, setting and design.
critical_limit: Heterogeneous interventions and outcomes; does not define one ideal quiz configuration.
p1_implication: Represent practice frequency, response format, feedback and repetition separately.

reference: Gonçalves, Muniz and Jaeger (2025), Retrieval Practice Versus Elaborative Encoding, DOI 10.1007/s10648-025-10076-6
scope: retrieval versus elaborative activities; 44 studies; 142 comparisons
key_finding: Retrieval had a small overall advantage; the advantage was conditional on corrective feedback and differed by response format and comparator.
critical_limit: Does not make retrieval universally superior to all active learning; task and comparator heterogeneity remain.
p1_implication: Practice mechanism and feedback availability must be independent parameters; no universal retrieval-only default.
access_status: publisher page and project extraction verified

reference: Pan and Rickard (2018), Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning, DOI 10.1037/bul0000151
scope: transfer from retrieval practice; 192 effects; 122 experiments
key_finding: Transfer benefits depended on response congruency, elaborated retrieval and initial performance.
critical_limit: Transfer categories and tasks were heterogeneous.
p1_implication: Record practice response, target assessment response, item equivalence and transfer objective separately.

reference: Eisenkraemer, Jaeger and Stein (2013), A Systematic Review of the Testing Effect in Learning, DOI 10.1590/1982-43272356201314
scope: recall and recognition practice
key_finding: Both recognition and recall can support retention; production often showed larger benefits and feedback can mitigate risks from incorrect options.
critical_limit: Earlier narrative corpus and confounding among response format and feedback.
p1_implication: Selected and constructed response must coexist; selected response requires feedback and distractor governance.

reference: Breuer, Scherndl and Ortner (2023), Effects of Response Format, DOI 10.1098/rsos.220456
scope: open versus closed achievement and aptitude assessment; 102 studies; 392 effects
key_finding: Open and closed scores were correlated but not interchangeable; closed formats generally produced higher scores.
critical_limit: Primarily measurement evidence, not direct learning-effect evidence; item equivalence varied.
p1_implication: Do not compare mastery thresholds or scores across response formats without explicit calibration.

reference: Sher et al. (2026), Very Short Answer Questions vs Multiple Choice Questions, DOI 10.1186/s12909-026-09359-5
scope: health-professions assessment; 3 studies; 6 cohorts
key_finding: VSAQ scores were generally lower than MCQ and may reduce cueing; discrimination and reliability findings were promising.
critical_limit: Small, domain-specific corpus with extreme heterogeneity in the initial analysis.
p1_implication: Short constructed response is a distinct candidate; lower scores must not be interpreted as worse learning.

reference: Mertens, Finn and Lindner (2022), Effects of Computer-Based Feedback, DOI 10.1037/edu0000764
scope: 77 experiments; 163 effect sizes; KR, KCR, elaborated and answer-until-correct feedback
key_finding: Elaborated feedback ranked most favorably for lower- and higher-order outcomes; correct-answer and answer-until-correct feedback were often beneficial; correctness-only was weaker.
critical_limit: Effects varied by prior knowledge, domain, test format and outcome.
p1_implication: Feedback result, correct response, elaboration and answer-until-correct must be separate values; correctness-only should not be the general formative default.

reference: van der Kleij, Feskens and Eggen (2015), Effects of Feedback in a Computer-Based Learning Environment, DOI 10.3102/0034654314564881
scope: 40 studies; 70 effects; item-based computer feedback
key_finding: Elaborated feedback showed larger average effects than correct-answer or correctness-only feedback.
critical_limit: Implementations and domains were heterogeneous; longer feedback is not automatically better.
p1_implication: Recommend concise actionable elaboration as the first formative profile while preserving other values.
access_status: detailed abstract and project extraction verified

reference: Kandemir et al. (2026), Impact of Feedback Timing, DOI 10.1007/s10648-026-10117-8
scope: 51 studies; 160 effects; computer-assisted learning
key_finding: Immediate versus delayed feedback had no average winner; educational level, domain and response-time constraints moderated results.
critical_limit: Few multi-day delays; moderator confounding limits causal interpretation.
p1_implication: Timing must be configurable with explicit delay unit and context; no universal immediate-or-delayed rule.
access_status: publisher abstract and methods summary verified

reference: Chang and Li (2019), A Relative Effectiveness Assessment of an Immediate Feedback Assessment Technique
scope: 35 answer-until-correct studies
key_finding: Answer-until-correct formats outperformed conventional multiple choice on average in the reviewed corpus.
critical_limit: Publication-bias and implementation variation; largely selected-response contexts.
p1_implication: AUC is a permitted retry-feedback sequence, not a universal practice rule.

reference: Butler, Karpicke and Roediger (2007), The Effect of Type and Timing of Feedback on Learning from Multiple-Choice Tests, DOI 10.1037/1076-898X.13.4.273
scope: standard correct-answer versus answer-until-correct; immediate versus delayed
key_finding: Corrective feedback supported delayed cued recall; type and timing interacted with test learning.
critical_limit: Laboratory prose tasks and multiple-choice focus.
p1_implication: Reveal and retry sequence must be represented rather than collapsed into attempt count.

reference: Butler, Karpicke and Roediger (2008), Correcting a Metacognitive Error, DOI 10.1037/0278-7393.34.4.918
scope: feedback after multiple-choice responses with confidence judgements
key_finding: Feedback corrected errors and also improved retention of correct low-confidence responses.
critical_limit: General-knowledge laboratory tasks; confidence elicitation adds interaction cost.
p1_implication: Feedback can be useful after correct answers; confidence is a later candidate, not required in every practice.

reference: Butler and Roediger (2008), Feedback Enhances Positive and Reduces Negative Effects of Multiple-Choice Testing, DOI 10.3758/MC.36.3.604
scope: immediate, delayed or no feedback after multiple-choice tests
key_finding: Immediate and delayed feedback improved correct retention and reduced later intrusion of distractors.
critical_limit: Laboratory passages and cued recall; not a full classroom synthesis.
p1_implication: Selected-response practice should support corrective feedback and avoid preserving distractor exposure without correction.

reference: Kang, McDermott and Roediger (2007), Test Format and Corrective Feedback Modify Long-Term Retention, DOI 10.1080/09541440601056620
scope: multiple-choice, short-answer, reading and corrective feedback
key_finding: Test format and corrective feedback jointly affected long-term retention.
critical_limit: Short controlled texts and delayed test; no institutional consequence model.
p1_implication: Response format and feedback are interacting but independent parameters.

reference: Sotola and Crede (2021), Regarding Class Quizzes, DOI 10.1007/s10648-020-09563-9
scope: 52 classroom samples; 7,864 students
key_finding: Frequent low-stakes quizzes were moderately associated with performance; effects were larger when quiz scores contributed to grades.
critical_limit: Many studies were associational; grade contribution may change participation and effort rather than learning mechanism alone.
p1_implication: Consequence and grade contribution must be explicit and separate from practice; grade contribution is allowed but not the self-directed default.

reference: Phelps (2019), Test Frequency, Stakes, and Feedback in Student Achievement, DOI 10.1177/0193841X19865628
scope: 149 studies; 509 effects; frequency, stakes and feedback
key_finding: Combined testing, stakes and feedback were associated with achievement; moderators included response format, education level and design.
critical_limit: Corpus spans a century, mostly English-language and US studies; nonrandom designs sometimes produced larger effects.
p1_implication: Frequency, stakes and feedback cannot be represented by one assessment mode; institutional profiles require separate decisions.

reference: von der Embse et al. (2018), Test Anxiety Effects, Predictors, and Correlates, DOI 10.1016/j.jad.2017.11.048
scope: 238 studies across educational outcomes
key_finding: Test anxiety was negatively related to performance; perceived difficulty and high-stakes consequences related to higher anxiety.
critical_limit: Predominantly correlational evidence; magnitude and populations vary.
p1_implication: High-stakes consequences require explicit profile, accessibility and risk treatment; no high-stakes default for personal practice.

reference: Leria, Benitez and Fraga (2021), Assistive Technology in Large-Scale Assessments, DOI 10.1007/s10639-020-10419-6
scope: 28 studies; visual impairment and computer-based assessment
key_finding: Computer-based assessment still presents major barriers; assistive technologies and construct-aware accommodations are necessary.
critical_limit: Large-scale assessment focus and visual impairment emphasis.
p1_implication: Response accommodations and assistive compatibility are structural requirements; accommodation must not be treated as cheating or ordinary preference.

reference: CAST (2024), Universal Design for Learning Guidelines 3.0
scope: learner variability; action and expression
key_finding: Guidelines recommend varying and honoring response methods, accessible tools, graduated support and action-oriented feedback.
critical_limit: Design framework, not an effectiveness estimate or assessment-validity rule.
p1_implication: ARA must allow accessible response alternatives and graduated support while recording construct implications.

reference: W3C WAI, WCAG 2.2 Input Assistance and Error Prevention
scope: forms, input validation, errors and reversibility
key_finding: Users need labels, accessible notifications, correction opportunities, confirmation and reversible submissions; time limits should be avoidable or extendable when nonessential.
critical_limit: General web interaction guidance, not a pedagogical parameter study.
p1_implication: Every response control and feedback state must be perceivable, correctable and assistive-technology compatible; time accommodation overrides ordinary defaults where required.

reference: Gao et al. (2023), Automatic Assessment of Text-Based Responses, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2308.16151
scope: 93 studies; post-secondary open-text assessment
key_finding: Automated assessment spans varied models and outputs, but validity, transparency and transfer remain uneven.
critical_limit: Preprint status in project corpus; technical accuracy does not establish educational authority or fairness.
p1_implication: Probabilistic scoring may assist but must not be authoritative by default; open response requires rubric, provenance and contestability.

reference: AraLearn source and documentation at commit 9bff37e
scope: self-directed mobile/offline study
key_finding: AraLearn uses low-consequence practice, deterministic gap/choice validation, answer reveal and structural completion while not recording attempts, correctness, errors or time.
critical_limit: One situated profile; current response mechanics are limited and exact attempt behavior is not a universal rule.
p1_implication: Preserve as reference profile: no grade or ranking, no attempt telemetry, structural progress and learner-controlled study.
access_status: source repository and canonical audit verified
